title: Effect of FeNb lump size and dissolution temperature on microstructure and properties of a Nb-stabilized austenitic stainless steel
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the influence of ferroniobium (FeNb) lump size and dissolution temperature on the dissolution kinetics, microstructure, and resulting mechanical and corrosion properties of a Nb-stabilized austenitic stainless steel (AISI 347). FeNb was added to an AISI 304 base steel under three distinct dissolution conditions involving variations in lump size (25–30 mm and 45–50 mm) and temperature (1560–1590 °C and 1610–1630 °C). Dissolution kinetics were monitored via time-resolved chemical analysis, while microstructural evolution was characterized by scanning electron and optical microscopy and thermodynamic simulations. Mechanical performance was assessed through tensile and impact testing, and corrosion resistance was evaluated via potentiodynamic polarization in chloride solution. Results indicate that lump size and dissolution temperature affect features such as niobium carbonitrides morphology, delta ferrite stability and austenitic matrix composition. These features strongly influence mechanical behavior, with the best combination of strength, ductility and toughness observed in the condition containing fragmented carbonitrides, retained delta ferrite and solid solution strengthening enhanced by niobium and silicon, yielded by coarse lump dissolution at lower temperatures. Corrosion resistance presented a complex dependence on these features, being strongly affected by the presence of microgalvanic cells. The findings highlight the critical role of dissolution conditions in tailoring the performance of Nb-stabilized stainless steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Ferroniobium (FeNb) alloy is used to add niobium (Nb) to steels. Nb exerts several positive effects to steels’ performance, mainly due to strengthening, both as solute and precipitate, and improving formability. However, it can also be used as a stabilizing element in low alloy and stainless steels to form stable carbides and carbonitrides, thus maintaining their corrosion resistance [ 1 ]. Regarding stabilization, Nb is preferred over titanium (Ti) because it forms carbides that are more stable and is easier to add to the matrix during steelmaking [ 2 ]. FeNb is fabricated by aluminothermic reduction in arc furnaces using pyrochlore concentrate, iron oxide (Fe 2 O 3 ), aluminum powder, lime and fluorite. Pyrochlore—(Na,Ca) 2 Nb 2 O 6 (OH,F)—is refined for impurity removal until there is only concentrated niobium oxide (Nb 2 O 5 ) left, which is then reduced through the aluminothermic route [ 3 ]. The molten ferroalloy is fed into molds and, after solidification, crushed down to lumps whose size distribution is defined upon sieving [ 4 5 ]. Aluminothermic reduction consists in reducing Nb 2 O 5  with aluminum, using energy from the reduction of Fe 2 O 3 . Fluorite and lime are usually used to decrease the melting point and viscosity of slag, facilitating its separation and increasing efficiency [ 6 ].

The standard FeNb alloy contains around 65wt% Nb. According to Cruz et al., its microstructure is formed by primary lamellae of the μ phase (Fe 21 Nb 19  or Fe 7 Nb 6 ) and eutectic zones composed by μ, Nb solid solution and a metastable Fe 2 Nb 3  phase [ 7 8 ]. The μ phase contains approximately 60wt% Nb and is relatively brittle, facilitating crushing of cast FeNb ingots into lumps, and Nb globules are enriched with this element in contents above 95wt% [ 5 ]. Shah, Henein e Ivey, on the other hand, observed only μ and Nb phases, being the first detected in two variations: one proeutectic with lower Nb content, corresponding to around 80% of the microstructure, and a eutectic enriched with Nb, accounting for approximately 10% of the alloy’s microstructure [ 9 ]. Observations made by Wang et al. also point out to a mixture of µ phase (around 58wt% Nb), Fe 2 Nb (45wt% Nb in average) and a terminal solid solution containing 96wt% Nb [ 10 ].

Ferroalloys can be divided into two classes, depending on the position of the melting interval with respect to the solidification temperature of steel. Dissolution mechanisms of both classes are considerably different. In both cases, a solid steel shell forms above their surface when they are added to liquid steel, and this shell proceeds to melt again, exposing the alloy. Class I alloys then dissolve rapidly, whereas class II alloys’ dissolution is slower, controlled by mass transfer between solid and liquid. Alloys like FeCr, FeMn, FeSi, SiMn belong to class I, because their melting intervals are below the solidification point of steels, while FeMo, FeNb, FeV e FeW belong to class II, with their intervals above steels’ solidification point [ 11 ].

The dissolution behavior of FeNb during steelmaking is not so frequently studied; The main works are those by Cruz et al. [ 7 8 ], with focus on the mechanisms of dissolution itself, with no correlation of dissolution parameters on the matrix properties. Although not so frequently studied, such phenomenon is of vital importance, especially to avoid the presence of undesired coarse precipitates that might hinder the steel’s performance, e.g., hot cracking during thermomechanical processing, ductility loss and welding-related issues [ 12 ]. Existing hypotheses state that these coarse particles form either during solidification, due to segregation, or originate from the addition of ferroalloys to the molten matrix, meaning that they would present already prior to solidification [ 3 12 ] Abraham et al. suggested that they would form by nucleation and growth due to solute enrichment during dissolution of elements, and FeNb’s high density and the formation of a solid shell on its surface at the moment of incorporation would favor their presence by retarding dissolution and promoting decantation [ 12 ]. Even though their study is vital to help understand the formation of coarse Nb-rich phases in steel, again, no advances were made in terms of process–microstructure–property correlation.

On one hand, smaller lumps have more surface area and higher heat capacity, accelerating dissolution and minimizing the dwell time of the solid shell. Moreover, again, FeNb is denser than steel, which might limit the use of coarser lumps. On the other hand, excessively small lumps can be easily entrapped by the slag of the molten bath [ 5 ]. Cruz et al. studied the dissolution of FeNb lumps with different sizes and verified that briquetted lumps dissolve faster than bulk ones and that the higher the temperature, the smaller the influence of lump size on dissolution kinetics, most likely due to superheating effects [ 7 ]. On some occasions, however, the presence of coarse carbides can be beneficial. In heat-resistant stainless steels, the formation of Nb carbonitrides with Chinese script morphology was considered responsible for an improved creep resistance, because this morphology is more effective to restrict slip along grain boundaries and strengthens interdendritic regions, in addition to enhancing thermomechanical fatigue resistance [ 13 14 ].

Nb-stabilized stainless steels are extensively used for lengthy applications in nuclear and oil and gas industries due to their enhanced corrosion resistance and higher mechanical strength as compared to other austenitic steels, especially at temperatures up to 427 °C (800°F). At higher temperatures, niobium takes part in important precipitation reactions that contribute greatly to the steel’s strengthening [ 16 ]. AISI 347 steel was specifically developed from AISI 304 as a response to austenitic steels’ susceptibility to sensitization [ 17 ]. Sensitization is the phenomenon through which chromium (Cr) carbides precipitate along grain boundaries, typically after long exposure to temperatures between 425 and 900 °C, leading to depletion of Cr in solid solution in the regions, making the material prone to intergranular corrosion. Since Nb forms more stable carbides and nitrides than chromium, it prevents sensitization by removing carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) from the solid solution [ 1 17 ]. AISI 347 stands virtually all types of atmospheres, except for reducing ones, and presents good performance when exposed to fresh water, sea water and oxidizing atmospheres in general [ 1 ]. In a comparative study for boiler applications, 347 steel outperformed 304, 316 and 321 steels, also in harsh environments containing ashes rich in alkaline sulfates, forming a resistant oxide scale on its surface [ 18 ].

As mentioned, the main existing works related to the subject are focused on the dissolution mechanisms of FeNb itself. In this context, this work evolves to the next step to evaluate the effects of dissolution conditions—FeNb lump size and dissolution temperature—on the properties of the matrix. Understanding such size vs. temperature interplay is extremely relevant in an industrial scenario continuously seeking process optimization to save resources and reduce waste. The present study was applied to an AISI 347 steel, produced by adding the ferroalloy to an AISI 304 steel base. Mechanical and corrosion properties were assessed for correlation with dissolution conditions.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
paragraphs: For this study, an AISI 304 austenitic stainless steel was used as the base material to which FeNb was added, aiming to produce an AISI 347 steel containing 1.0 wt% Nb. The compositions of the AISI 304 steel and ferroalloy used in this work, measured by the respective suppliers, are presented in Tables  1  and  2 , respectively. sections.heading: 2.2 Casting and heat treatment
paragraphs: Around 50 kg of AISI 304 steel was cast in an inductotherm transite box induction furnace with a graphite crucible. Temperature monitoring was carried out with an Italterm Fornero II immersion thermocouple. Three dissolution conditions were studied, as shown in Table  3 , and the rationale behind the definition of these conditions is as follows: A comparison was aimed between a dissolution condition using a standard lump size—25–30 mm—and conditions using coarser lumps—45–50 mm—at the same temperature and at a slightly higher one, to understand the likely effects of using a coarser raw material on steelmaking parameters. Regarding dissolution temperature, ranges were considered due to the difficulty to keep a constant value, especially after the introduction of FeNb lumps, which were not preheated. Moreover, different ferroalloys—low carbon Fe-61.5wt%Cr, low carbon Fe-78.35wt%Mn, Fe-29.25wt%Ni and Fe-75.98wt%Si—also at room temperature were eventually added to the melt for minor composition adjustments. Table 3 Studied dissolution conditions Condition FeNb lump size Dissolution temperature 01 45–50 mm 1610–1630 °C 02 45–50 mm 1560–1590 °C 03 25–30 mm 1560–1590 °C

The kinetics of FeNb dissolution were analyzed by taking small samples of liquid steel at 10 s, 30 s, 60 s, 100 s, 170 s and 240 s after the introduction of FeNb lumps, with the aid of a graphite crucible. Times for composition measurement were defined based on previous works focused on FeNb dissolution in steel. Chemical composition was measured in a calibrated GNR Metal Lab 75/80 J optical emission spectrometer.

After full dissolution, a ladle was used to transfer the melt from the induction furnace to the final sand mold. The ladle was heated using a gas furnace to prevent precocious solidification of material. The sand mold was designed according to ASTM A703 [ 20 ] to yield ingots with the geometry shown in Fig.  1 , which also indicates the positions where specimens for tensile testing (Specimen 3 of ASTM E8/E8M [ 21 ]) and impact testing (ASTM E23 [ 22 ]) were cut using electric discharge machining (and subsequent turning, in the case of tensile test specimens). Small pieces were also taken from the same regions for metallographic and corrosion analyses. Figure 1 Dimensions of the ingot cast according to ASTM A703 ( a ); positions chosen for machining of specimens ( b ).

Ingots were homogenized at 1150 °C for 5 h and air cooled in an Inforgel G11 muffle furnace before machining for comparison with the as-cast condition. The temperature was defined using Themo-Calc simulations (see section \* MERGEFORMAT 2.5), using as baseline a treatment time of 5 h, considering the size of the ingot. Besides 1150 °C, temperatures of 1050 °C and 1250 °C were evaluated. Figure  2 a shows the spatial phase distribution along the interdendritic region after 5 h at each temperature, while Fig.  2 b shows the elemental distribution. At 1250 °C, the formation of a considerably high amount of ferrite phase is predicted. The temperature of 1050 °C, in its turn, leads to higher levels of interdendritic segregation of Nb, C and N, meaning higher susceptibility to the formation of carbonitrides. Therefore, the intermediate temperature of 1150 °C was chosen. Figure 2 Phase distribution ( a ) and elemental distribution ( b ) as simulated by Thermo-Calc at each of the evaluated temperatures for the homogenization treatment after 5 h. FCC_A1: austenite; FCC_A1#2: Nb(C,N); BCC_A2: ferrite.

After machining, notch-free impact specimens were further heat-treated at 675 °C for 1 h for subsequent evaluation of the sensitization behavior, as recommended by ASTM A262 [ 23 ]. Sensitization treatments were done in a Gleeble® 540 thermomechanical simulator, which relies on resistance heating (Joule effect). A K-type thermocouple was welded onto the surface specimens at their mid-length position for temperature control. Treatments were carried out at ambient atmosphere, with a heating rate of 10 °C/min and air cooling.

sections.heading: 2.3 Characterization
paragraphs: The characterization plan is summarized in Table  4 . Table 4 Summary of experimental tests Material SEM OM Tensile testing Impact testing Corrosion testing FeNb X Conditions 01–03 as cast X Conditions 01–03 homogenized X X X X X Conditions 01–03 sensitized X X

Microstructural characterization involved scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and light optical microscopy (LOM). SEM was carried out in a Jeol JSM-56510LV microscope with a tungsten filament, equipped with a ThermoFisher® UltraDry energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector, operated at 20 kV. LOM was done in a Zeiss AxioScope.A1 microscope. The material was ground with progressively finer sandpapers, and final polishing was done with a 0.3 µm diamond suspension. To reveal the microstructure for LOM, specimens were etched with a 3:1 volume proportion mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid. For SEM, on the other hand, samples were not etched.

Mechanical characterization took place by tensile testing according to ASTM A370 [ 24 ] and Charpy (V-notch) impact testing according to ASTM E23 [ 22 ]. Tensile tests were done at room temperature in an Instron DL-2000 machine with load capacity of 20 kN with a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min. Impact tests took place in a Jinan Shidai Shijin Instruments JB-300AI/C machine, also at room temperature. Results shown hereby correspond to the average results of at least three valid tests.

sections.heading: 2.4 Electrochemical polarization
paragraphs: Potentiodynamic polarization tests were done in a Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT 128N potentiostat/galvanostat, on the cross-section surface of sensitized specimens, which were cut in the exact position of thermocouple placement (same area used for SEM analyses). Tests were started with surface stabilization in the electrolyte for 1 h (open-circuit potential–OCP). Afterward, tests were conducted with scanning speed of 10 mV/s within a potential range from − 1.5 V to + 1.5 V. All experiments were done in triplicate at room temperature. A three-electrode cell composed of an Ag/AgCl reference electrode, a Pt counter-electrode and the working electrode (test piece) was used, immersed in a 3.5% (m/V) NaCl electrolyte.

sections.heading: 2.5 Thermodynamic simulations
paragraphs: For a better understanding of the microstructural evolution, thermodynamic simulations were done using Thermo-Calc 2023a software with TCFE12 and MOBFE7 databases. Both equilibrium and Scheil calculations were carried out using an average of the composition obtained after casting (see Table  5 ), considering a nitrogen amount equal to the one shown in Table  1  for the base steel (0.094wt%). Simulations of the homogenization treatment were also done using the DICTRA module to define the best treatment temperature, as shown. sections.heading: 3.1. FeNb dissolution kinetics
paragraphs: The evolution of Nb concentration in the liquid matrix, representative of FeNb dissolution kinetics as influenced by lump size and temperature, is shown in Fig.  3 . It is important to emphasize that, in the present work, the dissolution has been evaluated in terms of the element incorporation by the matrix alone, since the main interest is in the final state of the material and its properties. A deeper understanding of the mechanisms involved in the dissolution requires the evaluation of phenomena such as mass transfer and solid shell formation, but this falls outside the scope of this study. The final compositions of the melt in each condition, right before feeding into the mold, are provided in Table  5 . Figure 3 Evolution of Nb concentration in the liquid steel (“Nb”) as function of time (“t”).

As expected, coarser FeNb lumps and lower temperatures delay dissolution. Furthermore, at higher temperatures, the evolution is well fitted by an exponential function, whereas lower temperatures lead to an approximately linear behavior. Full dissolution took longer than observed in the work by Cruz et al. [ 7 ]. However, caution is needed for direct comparison, since neither FeNb nor steel compositions are given by the authors; likewise, no information about melt agitation/homogenization is given. Interestingly, the kinetics are similar to previously predicted ones in static conditions [ 8 ]. Since melt agitation was achieved just by electromagnetic effects in the induction furnace, not as typically done in industrial conditions, with argon injection [ 26 ], dissolution may have been delayed due to a likely lower agitation intensity.

sections.heading: 3.2.1. FeNb alloy
paragraphs: Ferroniobium’s microstructure is depicted in Fig.  4 . It presents four distinct microconstituents with different compositions, as shown by semiquantitative EDS analyses compiled in Table  6 . The dark gray matrix corresponds to the µ (Fe 7 Nb 6 ) phase, the white phase consists in a Nb solid solution, and the black one is indicative of Fe 2 Nb (Laves’ phase). The light gray phase is disputed: Shah et al. [ 9 ] define it as a Nb-enriched µ phase, while Cruz et al. [ 8 ] claim it to be metastable ε-Fe 2 Nb 3  phase. Figure 4 FeNb alloy’s microstructure acquired by SEM using backscattered electrons’ signal with lower magnification ( a ) and higher magnification, with indication of EDS point analyses ( b ). sections.heading: 3.2.2. As-cast and homogenized steel
paragraphs: Microstructures of all three conditions, as cast and homogenized, are shown in Fig.  5  (condition 01), Fig.  6  (condition 02) and Fig.  7  (condition 03). To help identify these phases, a representative elemental map is provided in Fig.  8 . Overall, three phases can be observed. The light gray phase is the austenitic matrix, and two other secondary phases (white and dark gray) are seen mostly in boundaries. After homogenization, only the light phase remains in conditions 01 and 03, while condition 02 still presents the dark phase, even after heat treatment. Comparing homogenized and as-cast conditions, it can be observed that the lower dissolution temperature in conditions 02 and 03 leads to a microstructural state such that the homogenization treatment is less effective to dissolve secondary phases carbonitrides and even ferrite, when it comes to condition 02, as compared with the higher temperature in condition 01. Figure 5 Images acquired by SEM using backscattered electrons’ signal of the steel’s microstructure in condition 01 in as-cast and homogenized states. Figure 6 Images acquired by SEM using backscattered electrons’ signal of the steel’s microstructure in condition 02 in as-cast and homogenized states. Figure 7 Images acquired by SEM using backscattered electrons’ signal of the steel’s microstructure in condition 03 in as-cast and homogenized states. Figure 8 EDS elemental maps of phases observed in the fabricated steel.

The white phase is mostly enriched with Nb and Mo but also contains some Cr and Ni. This phase can be regarded as a niobium carbonitride, whose nature is highly disputed between an MX-type carbonitride, Nb(C,N), and the Z phase, (Cr,Nb)N. The presence of the latter in austenitic stainless steels is usually ascribed to the presence of Ni and Cr [ 27 ]. It can be found in 347 steels containing more than 0.06wt% N [ 27 ,  28 – 29 ]. It is, however, seldom reported and its stability and mechanisms of formation are little known. In terms of composition, while Sourmail [ 27 ] suggests that there is little or no substitutional dissolution in the Z phase, Dulieu [ 28 ] reports the existence of this phase containing Nb, Cr, Fe and Mo. Bajželjet al. [ 30 ], Xie et al. [ 31 ], and Yoon, Yoon and Lee [ 16 ], on the other hand, all describe the phase only as Nb(C,N). It was not possible to detect light elements, such as carbon and nitrogen, due to their extremely low amounts (order of ppm) associated with intrinsic limitations of the EDS technique to detect such elements. Particularly, there are MnS inclusions (black spots) associated with this phase, which have been previously observed as well and are denoted by the Mn map in Fig.  8  [ 30 ].

In fact, thermodynamic simulations carried out considering different nitrogen amounts—0.094wt% (Fig.  9 a) versus 0.01wt% (Fig.  9 b)—corroborate the effects of the element on the relative stability of the Z phase and of the carbonitride in equilibrium conditions. The Scheil profile (Fig.  9 c), however, indicates that only Nb(C,N) remains stable in the alloy during solidification, in addition to austenite and ferrite. Therefore, the observed phase can be regarded as a niobium carbonitride with a relevant dissolution of substitutional species, and its morphology varies from more continuous, thin films along boundaries in condition 01 to a Chinese script-like one in conditions 02 and 03, which become more fragmented after homogenization. Figure 9 Thermodynamic simulation results: equilibrium phases as function of temperature with N content of 0.094 wt% ( a ); equilibrium phases as function of temperature with N content of 0.01 wt% ( b ); Scheil solidification profile ( c ). FCC_A1: austenite; FCC_A1#2: Nb(C,N); BCC_A2: ferrite.

The dark phase, in its turn, corresponds to delta ferrite [ 30 32 ]. It is rich in iron (Fe) and chromium (Cr), followed by nickel (Ni), with approximate concentrations of 67-70wt% Fe, 21-27wt% Cr, 4-8wt% Ni and 1–1.5wt%Mo + Si, containing no or very few niobium. Table  7  shows the compositions of this phase in all conditions, in the as-cast state; curiously, it is enriched with Ni and Nb and lean in Cr and Mo in condition 02, with respect to conditions 01 and 03. Although Cr and Mo are also ferrite stabilizers, the additional enrichment with Nb appears to be enough to stabilize the phase upon heat treatment. With respect to the matrix, its composition in all conditions is shown in Table  9 . Attention must be given to the differences in Nb and Si concentrations between condition 02 and the others. In condition 02, the matrix is relatively enriched with both elements. Comparing it with condition 03, the higher Nb concentration in the matrix can suggest a retardation of the dissolution process by a possible entrapment of finer lumps in the slag on the surface of the molten steel. On the other hand, the lower enrichment in condition could also be explained by a delay in the dissolution process due to a higher thermal barrier to be overcome due to the steeper gradient formed in the frozen steel shell that forms when the ferroalloy is added to the molten matrix, as pointed out in the introduction. These results suggest that dissolution parameters in condition 02 lead to evident microstructural differences both in the as-cast state and after homogenization: the matrix enriched with Nb and Si and the presence of residual ferrite after heat treatment. sections.heading: 3.2.3. Sensitized steel
paragraphs: The microstructures of all three homogenized conditions after the additional sensitization treatment are shown in Fig.  10 . It can be suggested that the most visible contribution of this treatment was the decomposition of ferrite in condition 02, which can occur at temperatures as low as 600 °C [ 33 ]. Moreover, it has been shown that ferrite can decompose into austenite, carbides and other intermetallics, such as sigma and chi phases [ 33 34 ]; these intermetallics, however, were not found in the microstructure, at the same time that the amount of carbonitrides did not increase after the thermal cycle (see Table  8 ), meaning that ferrite transformed mainly into austenite. Figure 10 Images acquired by SEM using backscattered electrons’ signal of all conditions after the sensitization treatment.

sections.heading: 3.3. Mechanical behavior
paragraphs: Tensile tests’ curves of the homogenized steels are shown in Fig.  11 , while tensile and impact properties are summarized in Table  10 . Among all conditions, condition 02 presented the highest property values, especially elongation and impact energy. In fact, this condition, after casting and heat treatment, presented the closest properties to the ones required in standards such as the ASTM A276 (tensile strength of 515 MPa and elongation of 40% in the hot-finished state) [ 25 ]. Comparing conditions 01 and 03, the slightly lower strength in the first can be correlated with its lower amount of secondary phases, being predominantly composed by the soft austenitic matrix. Figure 11 True stress–strain curves of all conditions in the homogenized state. Table 10 Summary of mechanical behavior of all conditions in the homogenized state Condition Tensile strength (MPa) Elongation (%) Impact energy (J) 01 448,0 ± 4,9 31,5 ± 1,4 44,1 ± 10,5 02 504,9 ± 9,0 46,7 ± 5,5 66,0 ± 10,1 03 493,3 ± 5,2 37,6 ± 0,1 47,7 ± 5,9

For a better understanding of the alloy’s behavior, Fig.  12  is given, showing lower magnification OM images of all three homogenized microstructures. The observed behavior can be rationalized by a combination of Nb-rich carbonitrides and ferrite distribution, chemical homogeneity of the austenitic matrix, and the effectiveness of homogenization treatment in dissolving secondary phases, all affected by the heritage of FeNb dissolution conditions. These features directly control phenomena such as solid solution strengthening, precipitation and crack propagation. Figure 12 OM images of all conditions in the homogenized state.

As can be seen in Fig.  12  and recalling Fig.  5 , condition 01 has the lowest amount of residual secondary phases, no retained delta ferrite, and carbonitrides distributed in the form of thin films along boundaries. In this case, it can be assumed that the high dissolution temperature promoted better FeNb dissolution, reduced segregation and effective homogenization. With fewer and less effective crack blunting sites, deformation is more localized in the matrix boundaries. Then, strength would depend mainly on the relatively homogeneous austenitic matrix, with limited mechanisms to absorb impact energy. Xie et al. [ 31 ] showed that continuous networks of NbC are favorable to crack propagation, while fragmented and irregular morphologies, such as those shown in conditions 02 and 03, promote higher resistance to propagation, resulting in enhanced ductility.

Condition 03 presents a higher fraction of Nb(C, N) than condition 01, but in a fragmented form, and no retained delta ferrite either. In this case, FeNb dissolution could be more effective than in condition 02 due to the smaller lump size but is believed to be limited by the slag entrapment. Its strength is higher than in condition 01 but with comparable elongation and toughness, also lower than in condition 02. Results suggest that, although lump sizes were smaller in this case, the lower dissolution temperature still limited homogenization efficiency. The presence of fragmented carbonitrides contributes to local strengthening, increasing strength but also acting as stress concentrators, hindering ductility and impact energy absorption.

When it comes to condition 02, Fig.  12  depicts a higher concentration of carbonitrides, which are also fragmented. In this case, however, they are accompanied by delta ferrite islands (Fig.  6 ). The fact that this condition presented the highest strength and toughness suggests that the presence of ferrite is not harmful to the mechanical behavior of the alloy. In fact, it has been observed that delta ferrite can act to enhance ductility drastically, as observed by Muterlle et al. [ 35 ]. Although still not so studied in steels, it is a trending topic in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to rely on heterostructures to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, by the activation of mechanisms such as crack-tip blunting by tougher phases and enhancing the activation of slip systems to facilitate dislocation glide and reduce stress concentration [ 36 ,  37 – 38 ]. In this case, solid solution takes place as an additional strengthening mechanism, given the higher concentration of Nb and Si in the matrix, which are relatively strong solid solution strengtheners due to the atomic radius difference with respect to Fe’s radius [ 31 39 ], while ferrite can act as an additional obstacle to crack propagation, promoting crack deflection or branching, increasing the energy required for propagation.

Comparing the relative roles of carbonitrides and ferrite, the substantial strength enhancement from condition 01 to condition 03 suggests that carbonitride morphology plays a key role in defining strength levels for the material: A fragmented morphology is more efficient for strengthening. The fact that carbonitrides are more coherent with the matrix than ferrite further corroborates its main role [ 40 ]. The evolution from condition 03 to condition 02, in its turn, is much more significant from a ductility and toughness viewpoint, being influenced by the presence of Nb and Si in solid solution and of ferrite. In this case, solid solution can be regarded as an additional strengthening mechanism, as mentioned above, meaning that ferrite plays a crucial role to enhance energy absorption during deformation by crack deflection.

Figure  13  provides a schematic comparison of the mechanical behavior of all three conditions, summarizing all points that have been discussed above. Figure 13 Schematic representation of the mechanical behavior of the studied steel conditions.

sections.heading: 3.4. Corrosion behavior
paragraphs: The potentiodynamic polarization curves for the three studied conditions, before and after the sensitization heat treatment, are presented in Fig.  14 . Overall, the curves exhibit the characteristic electrochemical behavior of stainless steels, with the presence of active, passive and transpassive regions. It is important to emphasize that, even though corrosion potential is indicative of corrosion tendency, the passive behavior is strongly influenced by the stability and regeneration ability of the passive film. In stabilized steels, this stability depends on the homogeneity of the austenitic matrix, on the local availability of chromium in solid solution and on the distribution of carbonitrides [ 41 ]. Thus, the electrochemical behavior observed should be interpreted as a result of the interaction between chemical composition of the matrix, morphology of ferrite and carbonitrides and microstructural heterogeneity. Figure 14 Potentiodynamic polarization curves of all conditions: comparison between homogenized and sensitized states of condition 01 ( a ), condition 02 ( b ) and condition 03 ( c ); comparison between sensitized states of all three conditions ( d ).

After homogenization, condition 01 presented the highest corrosion potential (Ecorr = -0.68 V), indicating a more noble electrochemical behavior than conditions 02 (Ecorr = -0.87 V) and 03 (Ecorr = -0.93 V). This shift in potential toward more positive values suggests a lower thermodynamic tendency for anodic dissolution. After the end of the active region, the formation of an approximately constant current plateau can be observed, which is characteristic of the formation of a passive film on the surface of the material. The longer, more vertical and more stable this region is, the greater the tendency for the formation and maintenance of the passive film, which translates into higher resistance to both localized and generalized corrosion. Condition 01 also demonstrated the most stable behavior in the passive region. On the other hand, condition 03 presented a distinct behavior, characterized by the presence of two passive regions along the curve. Although this results in an apparently longer total passive region, it is observed that the formation of these regions occurs at significantly higher current density levels. This behavior suggests the formation of less protective or less stable passive films, possibly associated with electrochemical heterogeneities arising from the distribution of Nb(C,N), since no ferrite was observed in this condition after homogenization. While Nb acts as a stabilizing element, the presence of Nb(C,N) means that regions lean in Nb exist, and these regions are defective to generate and maintain passive films, becoming preferential sites for anodic dissolution. These heterogeneities can contribute to the occurrence of local differences in the stability of the passive film, leading to localized corrosion and making it difficult to maintain a uniform film.

After sensitization, none of the samples presented a clearly defined or stable passive region, indicating that the passive film formed on the surface could not remain continuous and homogeneous during polarization. According to Farahat and El-Bitar [ 39 ], the occurrence of intergranular sensitization can be qualitatively identified in polarization curves by the presence of secondary current peaks in the passive region, which indicate failures in the integrity of the passive film associated with the precipitation of chromium carbides at grain boundaries. However, in the conditions evaluated in this study, pronounced secondary peaks that clearly characterize the occurrence of this phenomenon were not observed. It is important to emphasize that no significant variations were observed in the chromium concentration in precipitates and matrix before and after sensitization, which is expected, since the role of Nb is precisely to promote the maintenance of Cr in solid solution. Likewise, the fraction of carbonitrides did not increase (Table  8 ). Therefore, a hypothesis involving the enrichment of carbonitrides with Cr is not likely to prove itself. However, a possibility exists that nanosized regions locally enriched in Nb and C may have formed after the treatment, promoting microgalvanic cells, intensifying the process of localized anodic dissolution.

The quantitative analysis of corrosion rates, obtained through the extrapolation of Tafel lines (Table  11 ), shows that conditions 01 and 02 exhibited an increase in corrosion rate after the sensitization treatment—144% and 416%, respectively—suggesting greater susceptibility to electrochemical dissolution under these conditions. Condition 02 presented the most critical increase. According to Peng et al. [ 42 ], in cast AISI 347H stainless steels, corrosion resistance is strongly dependent on the homogeneity of niobium and carbon distribution. In the homogenized state, this condition presents the smallest corrosion rate, suggesting that ferrite acts to improve the corrosion resistance of the material. In fact, previous works have concluded that ferrite is not harmful to the corrosion performance of stainless steels, but rather its decomposition, since it can lead to the formation of Cr- and/or Nb-depleted regions [ 43 ,  44 – 45 ]. After sensitization, it is likely that the sensitization treatment induced a Nb partitioning by the decomposition of ferrite, forming heterogeneous regions in the austenitic matrix that are not easily identified by microscopy but can act as microgalvanic cells. The absence of a stable passive plateau in the polarization curves for this sensitized sample corroborates the observations reported by Peng et al., indicating that the passive film may be discontinuous in these regions, which prevents its effective regeneration and accelerates the anodic dissolution process. Regarding conditions 01 and 03, opposed behaviors were observed, with condition 03 exhibiting a reduction of approximately 60% in its corrosion rate after the heat treatment, despite initially presenting significantly higher values. In this condition, a reduction in the amount of carbonitrides was estimated after the sensitization thermal cycle, while the carbonitride amount in condition 01 remained practically the same (Table  8 ). Since the carbonitride morphologies in both conditions were different, being more continuous in condition 01 and more fragmented in condition 03, the heat treatment may have caused the decomposition of smaller fragments in the latter, reducing the number of carbonitride/matrix boundaries and, consequently, regions that can act as microgalvanic cells. On the other hand, in condition 01, the opposite may have happened, reinforcing the hypothesis of formation of nanosized regions locally enriched in Nb and C. However, complimentary techniques such as high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, electrochemical impedance and double loop electrochemical potentiodynamic reactivation, would be necessary to confirm the raised hypotheses.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: FeNb dissolution kinetics are strongly affected by both lump size but mainly by temperature, with higher temperatures promoting faster niobium incorporation into the molten steel and lower temperatures slowing dissolution even for smaller lump sizes. Dissolution conditions lead to different chemical and microstructural features, including Nb- and Si-enriched matrix and retained delta ferrite in the condition with larger lump sizes dissolved at lower temperatures, even after the homogenization treatment, and a change in the morphology of carbonitrides from continuous films along boundaries at higher dissolution temperatures to a Chinese script-like shape at lower temperatures. Mechanical properties are governed by the interplay between matrix composition, carbonitride morphology and ferrite presence. The condition combining fragmented Nb(C,N) precipitates and residual ferrite exhibited the best balance of strength, ductility and impact toughness. Carbonitrides morphology and coherency with the matrix are vital to promote strength, while delta ferrite, often considered detrimental, can contribute positively to toughness by promoting crack deflection and increasing energy absorption during fracture. Results indicate that the corrosion resistance of the steel is governed by a complex interaction between factors such as the presence of secondary phases, phase morphology and chemical homogeneity of the matrix, which affect the stability of the passive film.

Overall, optimizing FeNb dissolution parameters is essential to control microstructure and achieve a balanced combination of mechanical performance and corrosion resistance in Nb-stabilized austenitic stainless steels. The present results are extremely relevant to the design of steelmaking in the sense of optimizing ferroalloys utilization by choosing coarser lumps, meaning less energy consumption during manufacturing and reduction of losses caused by the excessive formation of fines during mechanical crushing. Particularly, the study shows that lump size is not so critical to the dissolution kinetics at lower temperatures, suggesting that using coarse lumps does not necessarily result in the need of changing process parameters.
